subject: From South Africa to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You walked away from being the romcom king – turned down a $14.5 million check – because the quantity was all there and the quality wasn't. "Success without the profit" you called it. About a year ago your words kicked my ass and I've been repeating one line to myself ever since: f*ck the bucks, I'm going for the experience.
p2: Back in summer 2025, I read Greenlights – and the moment I closed the book, I made the decision to shut down the marketing agency I'd spent my life building; for years I wrote in other people's voices; The Wolf of Copywriting behind big names and brands. I could write in anyone's voice but my own. You spent years cast as a version of yourself that sold tickets but wasn't the whole man, then walked out to go find the real one. You did it on a scale I can barely imagine – but the boot that got me moving was yours. So I went all-in and bet everything on Mission: Meaning.

subject: Invite: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You listed Man's Search for Meaning as one of your favorite books. I named my podcast after it.
p2: You've written openly about the heaviness you carry - the sadness that hits hard on some days. I know a version of it. And I think the conversation underneath all your best ones is exactly that: how a human being keeps finding meaning anyway.

subject: From Vipassana to Man's Search for Meaning
p1: My Healing Journey After Childhood Abuse: ‘There’s light on the other side…”
p2: To this day, I remember finding your blog post while standing at the edge. I had just completed a Vipassana in the south of Thailand - which left me psychologically utterly destabilized and deeply, deeply depressed.

subject: Daring Greatly: An Invite to Man's Search for Meaning
p1: In 2007 you set out to prove that vulnerability gets in the way of success – and your own data broke you, then remade you. You called it a breakdown; your therapist called it an awakening. That's the crack I keep coming back to, long before the TED talk and everything it built…
p2: I come to this from my own crack in the middle of the road: a Vipassana that broke me open and left me in the dark for a long time, years of therapy and men's work since, and a childhood without a father, where being seen felt like the most dangerous thing there is. So the swamp you've spent two decades in – shame, vulnerability, the courage to be seen – is ground I've been walking too.

subject: From South Africa to San Francisco: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You went in as the most reluctant psychonaut alive – a card-carrying materialist, a child of the drug scare, sure the mystical was just neurons misfiring. And then your own self came apart into scraps of paper on the wind, and the man who trusted only what he could measure had to reckon with something the measurements couldn't hold. You've called yourself "spiritual but not religious" – and I keep wondering how the skeptic and the mystic in you have learned to live in the same mind…
p2: I come at this from the other side of the glass: How to Change Your Mind is a big part of why Germany’s #1 psychedelic therapy company I helped build even existed – we built it on the ground your work opened up. But where you came to the medicine as a reporter, I came through my own journey through the dark: the thing that broke and remade my whole life. So the frontier you mapped from the outside is one I've lived on.

subject: [Via Kyle Kingsbury] From South Africa to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You've spent your career learning how to add years to the end of a life. The harder thing, you've said, was learning how to actually want to be alive for them - after the rage you'd carried since childhood nearly cost you everything you loved…
p2: I built Germany's #1 psychedelic-therapy company, chased the next win relentlessly and used all of it to outrun a pain I never wanted to look at - until I burned out and hit rock bottom so hard that it almost broke me. What finally cracked me open was being forced to sit with everything I'd spent my whole life achieving my way around. That reckoning is the reason this show exists - and it's why your work on emotional health as the real foundation of a long life lands with me far harder than any protocol ever could.

subject: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: The Obstacle Is the Way. Stillness Is the Key.
p2: Your words didn't cure me. But The Obstacle Is the Way gave me a frame for the wreckage. And Stillness Is the Key gave me something to walk back toward, even after stillness itself had nearly destroyed me.

subject: From South Africa to LA: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: "Yet, in a bizarre, backwards way, death is the light by which the shadow of all life's meaning is measured."
p2: Like you, I've chased something across the globe: 35 countries, 5+ years of nomading through the continents, never quite able to sit still. And when I heard you'd walked away from your old podcast because you were done with the grandstanding, something landed – it's exactly why I do it the way I do: in-person only, no masquerade, only the real questions worth sitting in.

subject: Man's Search For Meaning
p1: You spent thirty years studying what makes a company great. Then you turned the same relentless questions on the only thing that finally matters – what makes a life.
p2: The question you spent a decade on for the new book is the exact one my whole show is built around. I come at it from the other end though – not the researcher's chair, but my own collapse in my twenties and the long climb back. Same summit, opposite routes.

subject: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: "I thought climbing the Devil's Thumb would fix all that was wrong with my life. In the end, of course, it changed almost nothing. But I came to appreciate that mountains make poor receptacles for dreams."
p2: You wrote that not about a character, but about yourself. I know that exact disillusionment from the other side of the world – I went looking for my own summit in a silent retreat, certain it would fix me, and it nearly destroyed me instead. Your line is the truest thing I've read about the search…

subject: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: "Most of us have two lives: the life we live, and the unlived life within us. Between the two stands Resistance."
p2: I've read all your books. And this very line found me at the exact moment I needed it. For years I lived the first life – “The Wolf of Copywriting”, writing in everyone's voice but my own. Copywriting was my shadow career, the proxy I hid in so I'd never have to risk the real thing. The War of Art is the book I'm living inside right now, page by page, as I finally try to write my own…

subject: Invite: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: At 18, you lost your best friend Harald to a car crash on an icy road. You've said you couldn't bring him back – but you could do something for all the others. So you gave the rest of your life to it: Stanley and Waymo – a vow to save a million people a year.
p2: I make a show about people who turned the worst thing that happened to them into a reason to build a life. You might be the purest version of that I've come across – a man who answered a death with a mission for the living.

subject: Taking The 3rd Door: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: A friend gifted me your book on Audible 5 days ago – said your journey and unconditional persistency reminded him of mine – and I binged the whole thing in a couple of sittings. And what's stayed with me since is the part most people skip right past: the darkness underneath the quest, the years it nearly took you out…
p2: Here's why it landed so hard: I'm running my own version of the Third Door right now. I've put my last savings on the table and flown all the way from South Africa to build this thing – a podcast I only ever record in person, talking my way past the line to people I've no business reaching yet. It's all in. And I know the hidden cost of a quest like that – the self-doubt and the rock bottom that never make the highlight reel.

subject: [Via Cal Callahan] From South Africa to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You've been buried twice: once by the cancer that was supposed to kill you at 25, and once by the world that crowned you a hero and then set out to erase you. Most men don't survive either. You walked out of both…
p2: I'd never claim to know what you've lived through - yours was a global scale, a whole different order than anything I've faced. But in my own small way I've built something, lost all of it and had to claw back from rock bottom. Which is why the arc of a man the whole world tried to write off stayed with me for years. And eventually became one of the inspirations to build this podcast.

subject: From South Africa to Texas: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You've preached to millions and built the Potter's House from nothing. And this year, after your own body sounded a warning, you placed it in your daughter's hands. I keep thinking about what that asks of a man – to let go of the very thing he built and became.
p2: I don't come from your tradition, but I come from my own wreckage – a breakdown that cracked me open and a long search for God through it. I grew up without a father, and it took a circle of men, years later, to show me what grace between men even looks like. So a life spent helping others carry what's too heavy to carry alone is something I hold with real reverence.

subject: [Via Danny Miranda] From South Africa to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: Long before you were teaching the internet to buy boring businesses, you were a reporter in Juárez - documenting cartel violence and human trafficking, close enough to the worst of it to win an RFK award. Then you walked away from telling the story, convinced that moving money would change more than words ever could…
p2: I know the pull of walking away from the respectable path to bet on your own; I left my career and marketing agency behind, flew across the world on my last savings to build one of the most impactful podcasts the world has ever listened to - because I'd rather own something true than keep renting out my voice in someone else's story. So the ownership gospel you preach is pretty much the north star my life is striving towards.

subject: From South Africa to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You wrote Unscripted for the 20 y/o version of you who was failing and desperately needed direction. It went on to reach the 21 y/o me in my senior year, sitting on a $100k soccer scholarship, staring down the safe, scripted life everyone begged me not to leave. But the moment I closed the book, I walked away from all of it. Years later, that one word became the whole spirit of the life I built – and of the podcast I now host: unfiltered, unpolished, unscripted…
p2: You were the earliest spark: long before the ashrams, the men's work, the psychedelics – there was a broke kid in a dorm reading a book that told him the Script was a lie he didn't have to live. That's the fork my entire life bent around. And the show I built runs on the exact code you handed me: no script, no polish, no safe answers – just the raw truth of how people actually became who they are.

subject: From South Africa to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You gave away tens of millions of shoes and became the poster child for business-as-good – and then spent two years so far down that they told you you were bipolar and put you on four medications that left you numb. A cactus and a vine did what the pills couldn't: they gave you back to yourself…
p2: I can't compare what I built to what you did – you did it maybe 400x bigger, but the shape is almost the same: I built a marketing agency alongside spiritual teachers and coaches, sure I'd finally found my purpose, that this was the meaningful thing – and I still ended up standing there empty. I know the psychedelic world from the inside too: years building Germany’s #1 therapy company, and a Vipassana that completely broke and left me in the dark for a long time. So the world you now pour $100M into is one I've lived inside.

subject: From South Africa to San Francisco: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You quit the thing you were best at at 15, and spent the next 15 years building a life that looked right from the outside. Then on the night you turned 30 you walked out of your own birthday party and ran until morning…
p2: I know that walk out of the door: I built the accomplishments too – a career that looked right and felt wrong – and then left a country over it. Mine turned into 35 countries chasing something I couldn't name. And the closest I've come to your kind of distance is a Vipassana that cracked me open into a spiritual emergency: 10 days of stillness going way past the point where everything in me wanted to stop.

subject: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You just wrote a whole book about the meaning crisis in young strivers: finding purpose in an age of emptiness. I'm one of the strivers you wrote it for – except I already walked through that emptiness and out the other side. Your book named a crisis I've been living…
p2: There's a parallel in your story I feel in my bones. You had the French horn – a gift that peaked young and a door that closed before you were ready. I had football; I left that career behind in my early twenties. I know what it is to be defined by a thing and then to have to find out who you are without it. Later I walked away from marketing “big names” and writing in other people's voices to build my own work – my own second curve, decades earlier than most people face it.

subject: From South Africa to San Francisco: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: The day your daughter was born, someone talked you into a client meeting – and you stood there in a suit, knowing you'd traded the one moment that actually mattered for a room that didn't. That fool's bargain became your life's work: helping the rest of us stop making it…
p2: I built my whole life around a version of what you teach: I walked away from the safer, more profitable path more than once – a football career, then my marketing agency – and bet everything I had on a podcast I only ever record IRL: depth over quantity, no chasing numbers, less but real. So "the disciplined pursuit of less" is the bet my whole life is on.

subject: From Cape Town to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: "I'm a 40-year-old grown man who has accomplished every goal I've ever set – and I'm not yet free."
p2: You wrote that about the father. Maybe the line of yours that touched me the most. I read it the week I decided my first darkness retreat – alone, in the mountains of Mexico – would be my initiation into becoming one. Because I know that exact lack of freedom and I know the wound underneath it.

subject: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You wrote that we picture awakening beginning with some mystical high – but that most people actually arrive on the path through loss, cracked open by what they never chose…
p2: That was me, exactly. I went looking for the high in a Vipassana in Thailand and instead it detonated something I'd spent my life outrunning and left me in the dark for a long time. For a while I was sure I was the only one it had broken – that I'd failed at the one thing meant to bring peace. Then I found your conversation with Tim Ferriss, and heard him name the exact terror I'd been carrying alone. I wasn't crazy. I wasn't the only one.

subject: Man's Search For Meaning
p1: You were agnostic your whole life – until your divorce, your mom's cancer and your dad's collapse stacked up all at once, and somewhere in that pile-up of pain you found God…
p2: I named this show after Frankl's work; meaning found inside suffering. Your conversion reads almost like a case study in it: you didn't reason your way to God, you got broken into it. I've walked the same road: A Vipassana in my early twenties dropped me into a depression I wasn't sure I'd survive, along with losses I still carry – children gone before they were born. That wreckage is what finally brought me to God.

subject: From South Africa to San Francisco: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You've mapped the machine better than anyone alive: dopamine, sleep, cold, light, the protocols for running a human well. But a perfectly optimized body still has to answer the oldest question there is: what is all of it for? Every big show camps out in the mechanism. I'm here for the meaning underneath it…
p2: Your work pulled me out of a depression: the light, the sleep, the cold, the discipline I borrowed from you became the scaffolding I rebuilt my life on. And then I hit the deeper problem: I had a body that finally worked and a life I still had to find a reason to live. That gap – between a well-run life and a meaningful one – is why I started this podcast in the first place:

subject: From South Africa to America: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: In 2011 you were on the floor after one night too many, feeling your life run out and begging to keep it. What you did with the 2nd chance is the reason I'm writing: you sat down with everything you'd spent your life running from – and slowly turned it into a life's work…
p2: We come from the same practice: a Goenka Vipassana in the South of Thailand broke me apart in my early 20s, and the years of sitting afterward were survival long before they were ever peace. I've lived in the plant-medicine world too, built Germany’s #1 psychedelic therapy platform and guided hundreds of people through their own voyages. So the ground you write from – the wreckage, the radical honesty, the slow way back – is the ground I've walked too…

subject: Inspired by Seek Discomfort: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: A kid from South Africa, a one-way ticket and a big American Dream - inspired by Yes Theory and Seek Discomfort…
p2: And I mean it: you four are part of why it exists. Through some of my darkest years it was your voices in my ears - say yes, seek the discomfort, the life you want is on the other side of the thing that scares you most.

subject: [Via Pat Killoren] From Cape Town to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: You've said one of the gifts of cancer was that it freed you to run for office – that facing your own mortality gave you the urgency to build a life of service. That line is the reason I'm writing you…
p2: I've just landed in Austin – your city – to go all-in on my dreams and everywhere I go I keep meeting the soul of the place. I come at meaning from my own edge: a collapse that made me lose everything in a matter of weeks and a long climb back. So a man who found his life's direction staring down his own death is exactly who this show exists for.

subject: From South Africa to Austin: Man's Search for Meaning
p1: Halfway through 2nd grade, your daughter came home and told you school was boring – and instead of shopping for a better school, you decided the whole 200-year-old model was broken and set out to tear it down. That decision is what I can't stop thinking about…
p2: I come at this as exactly the kid the system had no idea what to do with: I struggled with authority my whole life, got kicked out of more than one school and ultimately dropped out of college in my senior year. Everything that model is built to grind down, I ran straight into – and came out the other side building a life that's genuinely my own. So a woman tearing that system apart is exactly the kind of person this show exists for…

subject: Man's Search for Meaning, AfrikaBurn & BurningMan
p1: Every interview hands you the same question in a new costume – the mud, the money, the ticket prices, "Is Burning Man over?" But underneath all of it sits one real question: can a culture outlive the people who dreamed it. You're the one who has to answer that – you were in the room when Larry died. Every big show stops at the spectacle. I'm only here for the question underneath…
p2: I came to my first AfrikaBurn for the craziest party of my life – but one week in the Tankwa dust turned it into a rite of passage: I let go of my business, dropped the mask and started this podcast. The Regional Network you built rerouted my whole life…
